title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
text:
“Philosophy is written in this grand book, the universe … It is written in the language of mathematics, and its characters are triangles, circles, and other geometric figures.”
– Galileo Galilei, Il Saggiatore
The first time you meet an elliptic curve, the name is almost actively unhelpful. It is not an ellipse. It is not even especially curved in the way a circle is curved. It is a cubic equation pretending to be a drawing.
Here is the version I want you to hold in your head: \[
E: y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B.
\tag{1}\] For now work over the real numbers, and assume the curve is smooth, meaning \[
4A^3 + 27B^2 \ne 0.
\tag{2}\] That condition is the small print that prevents the curve from pinching into a cusp or crossing itself.
The surprise is that the points on this curve can be added. Not approximately. Not metaphorically. Added, as an abelian group. The rule is so visual that it feels at first like a drawing trick: take two points, draw a line, find the third intersection, and flip it.
That is the whole machine. Everything else in this post is bookkeeping to explain why the machine is honest.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
text:
First, draw the addition
Take two points \(P\) and \(Q\) on the curve. Draw the straight line through them. A line and a cubic curve usually meet in three points, so after \(P\) and \(Q\) there is one more point. Call it \(R\).
Now reflect \(R\) across the \(x\)-axis. The reflected point is, by definition, \[
P + Q.
\]
That sounds like a magician naming the rabbit after pulling it from the hat. But pause on the picture. We are not choosing a third point freely. The line is forced by \(P\) and \(Q\); the cubic supplies the missing intersection; the reflection is the only extra convention.
Here is a concrete curve where the drawing can be done by hand: \[
y^2 = x^3 - x + 1.
\tag{3}\] The points \(P=(0,1)\) and \(Q=(1,1)\) both lie on it. The line through them is the horizontal line \(y=1\). Substitute \(y=1\) into Equation 3: \[
1 = x^3 - x + 1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x^3 - x = 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x(x-1)(x+1)=0.
\] The three intersections have \(x=-1,0,1\). Two of them were \(P\) and \(Q\). The third is \(R=(-1,1)\), so \[
P+Q=(-1,-1).
\]
No formula found that point. The picture did.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def rhs(x):
    return x**3 - x + 1

x = np.linspace(-1.45, 1.75, 500)
y2 = rhs(x)
mask = y2 >= 0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.2))
ax.plot(x[mask], np.sqrt(y2[mask]), color="#244C5A", lw=2)
ax.plot(x[mask], -np.sqrt(y2[mask]), color="#244C5A", lw=2)
ax.axhline(1, color="#A85D32", lw=1.8, linestyle="--")

points = {
    "P": (0, 1),
    "Q": (1, 1),
    "R": (-1, 1),
    "P+Q": (-1, -1),
}
for label, (px, py) in points.items():
    ax.scatter(px, py, s=45, color="#A85D32")
    ax.annotate(label, (px, py), xytext=(7, 7), textcoords="offset points")

ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
ax.set_xlim(-1.45, 1.75)
ax.set_ylim(-1.6, 2.2)
ax.set_xlabel("$x$")
ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
ax.set_title("$y^2 = x^3 - x + 1$")
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.show()




On y^2 = x^3 - x + 1, the line through P=(0,1) and Q=(1,1) meets the curve again at R=(-1,1). Reflecting R gives P+Q=(-1,-1).




The picture is the writing highlight of the whole post: addition appears as a consequence of incidence. Arithmetic is hiding in the fact that a straight line cannot quite escape a cubic.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
section: Why a cubic gives a third point
text:
Why a cubic gives a third point
Let us say the algebra out loud, because this is where the rule stops being a doodle.
A non-vertical line has equation \[
y = mx + c.
\] Substitute this into Equation 1: \[
(mx+c)^2 = x^3 + Ax + B.
\] After moving everything to one side, this is a cubic equation in \(x\).
A cubic has three roots when counted with multiplicity and over an algebraic closure. Geometrically: a line meets a projective cubic in three points, with tangency counted twice. This is the mild form of Bezout’s theorem sitting underneath the drawing [1], [2].
So if the line already goes through \(P\) and \(Q\), the third intersection is not an artistic choice. It is the remaining root of a cubic equation.
There are two special cases, and neither is an exception.
If \(P=Q\), the secant line has collapsed into a tangent line. The tangent counts as meeting the curve twice at \(P\), so there is still a third intersection. Reflect it, and you get \(2P\).
If the line is vertical, it goes through \(P=(x,y)\) and its mirror \(-P=(x,-y)\). The third point is not finite. It is the point at infinity, which we call \(O\).
That last sentence is the part that usually feels suspicious, so let us slow down.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
section: Why infinity has to be there
text:
Why infinity has to be there
The curve Equation 1 is easier to manage if we add one extra point: \[
O = \text{the point at infinity}.
\] In projective coordinates, the short Weierstrass curve has exactly one such point, written \([0:1:0]\).
This is not decorative. It repairs the three-intersections rule.
A vertical line through \(P\) and \(-P\) has already used up two finite intersections. The third intersection is \(O\). With that convention, the chord rule says \[
P + (-P) = O.
\] So \(O\) behaves exactly like zero should behave: it is what you get when you add a point to its inverse.
This is the same kind of move the blog keeps returning to. Residues became coordinates in the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Configuration spaces made rectangles visible. Here, one extra point at infinity makes a broken geometric rule whole.
Once \(O\) is admitted, every line meets the cubic three times, and the addition rule has somewhere to send every case.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
text:
The group law
Now we can state the result cleanly.

Theorem 1 (Elliptic Curve Group Law) Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic not \(2\) or \(3\), and let \[
E: y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B
\] with \(4A^3 + 27B^2 \ne 0\). Add the point at infinity \(O\). The chord-and-tangent rule makes \(E(K)\) into an abelian group with identity \(O\).

Most of the group axioms are visible.
The identity is \(O\). A finite point \(P=(x,y)\) has inverse \(-P=(x,-y)\). Commutativity is built in: the line through \(P\) and \(Q\) is the same line through \(Q\) and \(P\).
Associativity is the hard axiom: \[
(P+Q)+R = P+(Q+R).
\] Do not let anyone wave this away as “obvious from the picture.” It is true, but it is not locally visible in one chord. Standard proofs use projective geometry, divisors, or explicit algebraic verification; Silverman and Tate give a friendly path into this theorem [2].
That honesty matters. The picture discovers the rule. The theorem proves that the rule can carry arithmetic.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
section: The formulas are the shadow of the picture
text:
The formulas are the shadow of the picture
The drawing is primary, but computation needs coordinates.
For distinct non-inverse points \(P=(x_1,y_1)\) and \(Q=(x_2,y_2)\), the slope is \[
\lambda = \frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}.
\] Then \[
x_3 = \lambda^2 - x_1 - x_2,\qquad
y_3 = \lambda(x_1-x_3)-y_1,
\] and \(P+Q=(x_3,y_3)\).
For doubling, the secant slope becomes the tangent slope: \[
\lambda = \frac{3x_1^2 + A}{2y_1}.
\] The same formulas for \(x_3\) and \(y_3\) then give \(2P\).
These formulas are not a second definition. They are the chord-and-tangent picture written in coordinates.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
section: Move the picture onto a finite clock
text:
Move the picture onto a finite clock
Now replace real numbers by residues modulo a prime \(p>3\). The same equation becomes \[
E(\mathbb{F}_p): y^2 \equiv x^3 + Ax + B \pmod p.
\] The points are now a finite set. There is no smooth curve to draw, only scattered dots on a modular grid.
But the algebraic rule survives. Division means modular inverse. Reflection means replacing \(y\) by \(-y \bmod p\). The same formulas still define addition as long as \[
4A^3 + 27B^2 \not\equiv 0 \pmod p.
\]
This is where the earlier discrete-log post re-enters. Pick a point \(P\) and keep adding it to itself: \[
P,\;2P,\;3P,\;\ldots,\;nP.
\] Going forward is fast by double-and-add. Given \(P\) and \(nP\), recovering \(n\) is the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem.
We have changed the clock. In the old post, the clock was the multiplicative group modulo a prime. Here the clock is a finite set of points on a cubic. The same asymmetry returns: forward is a stroll, backward is a search.
Koblitz and Miller independently proposed using this arithmetic for public-key cryptography in the 1980s [3], [4]. The security claim is still a hardness assumption, not a theorem. That distinction is part of the honesty of the subject.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
text:
A tiny finite-field check
Here is the smallest useful version of the arithmetic. No finite-field class. No protocol library. Just tuples and the group law.
Work on \[
E: y^2 = x^3 + 2x + 3 \pmod {97}.
\] The point \(G=(91,58)\) lies on the curve. It has order \(50\), so adding it to itself eventually walks through a small cyclic subgroup and returns to \(O\).
Do not read security into these numbers. The prime is tiny, the curve is arbitrary, and an attacker could exhaust the whole group by hand. The point is only to see the same law running on a finite clock.

p = 97
A = 2
B = 3
O = None

def on_curve(P):
    if P is O:
        return True
    x, y = P
    return (y*y - (x*x*x + A*x + B)) % p == 0

def neg(P):
    if P is O:
        return O
    x, y = P
    return (x, (-y) % p)

def add(P, Q):
    if P is O:
        return Q
    if Q is O:
        return P

    x1, y1 = P
    x2, y2 = Q

    if x1 == x2 and (y1 + y2) % p == 0:
        return O

    if P == Q:
        lam = (3*x1*x1 + A) * pow(2*y1, -1, p) % p
    else:
        lam = (y2 - y1) * pow(x2 - x1, -1, p) % p

    x3 = (lam*lam - x1 - x2) % p
    y3 = (lam*(x1 - x3) - y1) % p
    return (x3, y3)

def mul(n, P):
    result = O
    addend = P
    while n:
        if n & 1:
            result = add(result, addend)
        addend = add(addend, addend)
        n >>= 1
    return result

G = (91, 58)
assert on_curve(G)
assert add(G, O) == G
assert add(G, neg(G)) is O
assert mul(50, G) is O

for n in range(1, 9):
    print(f"{n}G = {mul(n, G)}")

1G = (91, 58)
2G = (74, 20)
3G = (83, 74)
4G = (24, 2)
5G = (73, 83)
6G = (46, 25)
7G = (39, 6)
8G = (65, 65)


And because associativity is the dangerous axiom, let the machine check it on this toy curve.

points = [O]
for x in range(p):
    for y in range(p):
        P = (x, y)
        if on_curve(P):
            points.append(P)

for P in points[:20]:
    for Q in points[:20]:
        for R in points[:20]:
            assert add(add(P, Q), R) == add(P, add(Q, R))

print(f"{len(points)} points on the curve, including O")
print("associativity checked on the first 20 points in each slot")

100 points on the curve, including O
associativity checked on the first 20 points in each slot


This is the skeleton ECC needs: \[
kG.
\] Given \(k\) and \(G\), computing \(kG\) is fast. Given \(G\) and \(kG\), recovering \(k\) is the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
text:
What ECC actually does
Elliptic-curve cryptography is not “encrypting with an elliptic curve.” That phrase hides the useful division of labor.
ECC gives you compact public-key operations. It is normally used for two jobs:

key agreement, where two parties derive a shared secret;
signatures, where one party proves that a message came from a private scalar.

For encryption, the usual pattern is hybrid. Use elliptic-curve key agreement to derive symmetric keys, then use authenticated encryption for the data. The curve does not replace the symmetric cipher. It gives the symmetric cipher a fresh key.
That is why the group law matters. The public operation is scalar multiplication: \[
kG = \underbrace{G + G + \cdots + G}_{k\text{ times}}.
\] The private object is the scalar \(k\). The public object is the point \(kG\).
The analogy with ordinary Diffie-Hellman is exact in shape. Replace modular exponentiation \(g^a\) with scalar multiplication \(aG\). The hard reversal changes name, but the asymmetry is the same.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
section: ECDH: a shared point without sending the secret
text:
ECDH: a shared point without sending the secret
Suppose Alice chooses a private scalar \(a\) and Bob chooses a private scalar \(b\).
Alice publishes \[
A = aG.
\] Bob publishes \[
B = bG.
\]
Alice can compute \[
aB = a(bG) = abG.
\] Bob can compute \[
bA = b(aG) = abG.
\] They arrive at the same point without sending either private scalar.
Here it is on the toy curve. Again: this is a teaching model, not a protocol.

alice_secret = 17
bob_secret = 29

alice_public = mul(alice_secret, G)
bob_public = mul(bob_secret, G)

alice_shared = mul(alice_secret, bob_public)
bob_shared = mul(bob_secret, alice_public)

assert alice_shared == bob_shared
print(f"Alice public key: {alice_public}")
print(f"Bob public key:   {bob_public}")
print(f"Shared point:     {alice_shared}")

Alice public key: (27, 7)
Bob public key:   (38, 90)
Shared point:     (39, 91)


Real ECDH has more ceremony. You validate or decode public keys according to the curve and protocol. You feed the shared value into a KDF. You bind the transcript, identities, and algorithm choices. You never treat a raw curve coordinate as the final encryption key.
The equation \(abG\) is the heart. The protocol is the body that keeps the heart alive under attack.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
section: Signatures: proving possession of the scalar
text:
Signatures: proving possession of the scalar
Signatures use the same private-scalar idea, but the goal changes.
For key agreement, the scalar helps two parties derive a secret. For signatures, the scalar lets one party produce a public proof tied to a message.
ECDSA and EdDSA are the two names you will see most often. Both live on elliptic-curve groups. Both publish a public key derived from a private scalar. Both verify a short signature using public arithmetic.
The practical difference is not just notation.
ECDSA is widely deployed and appears in standards, certificates, and hardware. It is also famously unforgiving about nonce generation. Reuse or bias the per-message nonce, and the private key can leak.
EdDSA, especially Ed25519, was designed to make the common case harder to misuse. It uses Edwards curves and deterministic signing as specified in RFC 8032 [5]. That does not make all implementations safe, but it removes one historic foot-gun.
This is the right mental split:

ECDH/X25519 answers “can we agree on a secret?”
ECDSA/EdDSA answers “did the holder of this private key sign this message?”

The group law is shared. The protocol purpose is different.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
section: Production parameters: what I would choose in 2026
text:
Production parameters: what I would choose in 2026
Production cryptography is not the place to be original. Do not invent curves. Do not choose a random point. Do not ship the formulas from this post. Use vetted protocol libraries and standard domain parameters.
As of June 29, 2026, my default choices would be:
X25519 and X448 are the Montgomery-curve choices specified for modern key exchange in RFC 7748 [6]. They are the reason many contemporary APIs expose “X25519” rather than asking you to select raw Weierstrass parameters.








Need
Default choice
When to choose something else




Modern key agreement
X25519
Use X448 when your ecosystem requires a larger classical margin. Use NIST P-256/P-384 when compliance or protocol compatibility requires it.


Modern signatures
Ed25519
Use Ed448 for a larger margin. Use ECDSA with P-256/P-384 when certificates, FIPS profiles, or legacy integrations require it.


Broad TLS compatibility
X25519 and secp256r1
Let the TLS stack negotiate from its supported groups. TLS 1.3 names X25519 and NIST curves among its supported groups [7].


FIPS-oriented deployments
P-256, P-384, or P-521 with approved algorithms
Follow FIPS 186-5 and NIST SP 800-186 rather than a blog table [8], [9].



The rough security-level map is:



Classical security target
Typical ECC family




about 128-bit
X25519, Ed25519, P-256


about 192-bit
P-384


about 224-bit
X448, Ed448


about 256-bit
P-521



These rows are not interchangeable promises. They are engineering landmarks. Real security also depends on implementation quality, side-channel resistance, randomness, key validation, protocol binding, and update discipline.
If you only remember one production rule, remember this:

Choose the curve through the protocol, not around it.

For TLS, SSH, age, Signal-style protocols, JWT libraries, certificates, hardware modules, and cloud KMS products, the protocol and platform usually narrow the correct answer. The best parameter choice is often the boring one that your audited stack already implements correctly.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
section: The checks that matter in real systems
text:
The checks that matter in real systems
A production ECC review should ask questions that do not appear in the pretty group-law picture.
Is scalar multiplication constant-time with respect to secret scalars? Are private scalars generated by a real CSPRNG or derived exactly as the standard says? Are ECDSA nonces deterministic or generated without bias? Are public keys validated or decoded under the curve’s rules?
Does ECDH feed a KDF with the right context, including transcript and algorithm identifiers? Does the protocol authenticate the peer, or is it only giving you an unauthenticated shared secret? Are signatures domain-separated so the same key cannot be tricked across protocols?
Are keys rotated and stored in hardware or a managed KMS when the threat model requires it? Is the dependency receiving security updates? Is the migration story clear if the ecosystem moves from classical ECC to hybrid post-quantum key establishment?
The last question is no longer theoretical planning. ECC is not quantum-safe. NIST standardized ML-KEM in FIPS 203 for post-quantum key encapsulation [10]. For long-term confidentiality, prefer standards-track hybrid or post-quantum options when your protocol stack supports them.
That does not make ECC obsolete overnight. It means ECC should be treated as part of a living cryptographic system, not as a timeless charm.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
section: How the whole machine fits together
text:
How the whole machine fits together
The path from the drawing to production is long, but it is not mysterious.
Start with a cubic. Add the point at infinity. Use chords and tangents to define addition. Move the arithmetic to a finite field. Pick a standard base point on a standard curve. Keep the scalar private. Publish the scalar multiple.
For ECDH, two scalar multiplications meet at the same point: \[
a(bG)=b(aG).
\] For signatures, the private scalar produces a proof that public arithmetic can verify.
The writing highlight is that the same geometric sentence keeps surviving translation:

A line meets a cubic one more time than you already accounted for.

On paper, that gives a reflected third point. In a finite field, it gives a group operation. In cryptography, repeated addition gives a one-way public-key primitive.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
text:
What to remember
An elliptic curve becomes arithmetic because a line and a cubic conspire to produce a third point. Reflect that point, add one point at infinity, and the drawing becomes an abelian group.
Over finite fields, the same rule turns scattered modular points into a finite group. Repeated addition is fast; reversing it is the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem.
ECC uses that asymmetry for key agreement and signatures. In production, the right answer is not a clever curve from scratch. It is a standard curve, a vetted library, a protocol-level KDF or signature scheme, and a clear migration plan for the post-quantum era.
Geometry has become a one-way door. Engineering decides whether the door is actually locked.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve, Drawn by Hand
text:
How to cite

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
“Mathematics is the art of giving the same name to different things.”
— Henri Poincaré
Here is a claim that sounds almost too clean to be true. Take any real symmetric matrix, no matter how tangled its entries look, and there is always a way to turn your head so that the transformation it describes does nothing fancy at all. It just stretches space along a set of perpendicular axes, each by its own amount. No shearing, no twisting, no mixing of directions. That is the whole content of the spectral theorem, and the rest of this post is about why space has no choice but to behave this way.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
First, the picture
Picture a linear map in two dimensions. In general it can do unpleasant things: it can rotate, it can shear a square into a slanted parallelogram, it can stretch more in one diagonal direction than another. A generic matrix really does mix your coordinate axes together.
Symmetry is the condition that quietly forbids all of that mixing, once you look from the right angle. The promise of the theorem is that for a symmetric matrix you can always find a fresh set of axes, still perfectly perpendicular to one another, in which the map becomes a pure diagonal stretch. Finding those special axes is the whole game, and they are exactly the eigenvectors.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
Setting it up
Let \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, meaning \(A^\top = A\). Write the standard inner product as \(\langle x, y\rangle = x^\top y\). The single fact that powers everything below is that symmetry lets you slide \(A\) from one side of an inner product to the other:
\[
\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle \qquad \text{for all } x,y \in \mathbb{R}^n.
\tag{1}\]
This is worth a moment. It says \(A\) treats both slots of the inner product identically, a property called self-adjointness. Everything that follows is really Equation 1 wearing different costumes.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
The theorem

Theorem 1 (Spectral Theorem) If \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric, then there exist an orthogonal matrix \(Q\) (so \(Q^\top Q = I\)) and a real diagonal matrix \(\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\) such that \[
A = Q \Lambda Q^\top .
\tag{2}\] Equivalently, \(\mathbb{R}^n\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of \(A\), and every eigenvalue is real.

Read Equation 2 from right to left and it tells the same story as the picture. The matrix \(Q^\top\) rotates you into the special axes, \(\Lambda\) does the honest diagonal stretching, and \(Q\) rotates you back. We reach it through two small observations.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
Two small facts

Lemma 1 (Eigenvalues are real) Every eigenvalue of a real symmetric \(A\) is real.


Proof. Let \(Ax = \lambda x\) with \(x \neq 0\), where for the moment we allow \(\lambda\) and \(x\) to be complex. Write \(x^{*}\) for the conjugate transpose, so \(\langle x, x\rangle = x^{*}x = \|x\|^2 > 0\). Because \(A\) has real entries and \(A^\top = A\), it is Hermitian: \(A^{*} = A\). Now follow a single quantity, \(x^{*}Ax\), down two different paths: \[
\lambda\, \langle x, x\rangle = x^{*} A x = x^{*} A^{*} x = (Ax)^{*} x = \bar\lambda\, \langle x, x\rangle .
\] The first equality uses \(Ax = \lambda x\); the middle uses \(A^{*}=A\); the last uses \(Ax = \lambda x\) again, now inside the conjugated slot. Since \(\langle x, x\rangle > 0\) we may cancel it, leaving \(\lambda = \bar\lambda\). A number equal to its own conjugate is real. \(\qquad\blacksquare\)


Lemma 2 (Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal) If \(Ax = \lambda x\) and \(Ay = \mu y\) with \(\lambda \neq \mu\), then \(\langle x, y\rangle = 0\).


Proof. Slide \(A\) across the inner product using Equation 1: \[
\lambda \langle x, y\rangle = \langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle = \mu \langle x, y\rangle .
\] Therefore \((\lambda - \mu)\langle x, y\rangle = 0\), and since \(\lambda \neq \mu\) the only way out is \(\langle x, y\rangle = 0\). The special axes are automatically perpendicular, exactly as the picture demanded. \(\qquad\blacksquare\)

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
Putting it together
We now assemble the theorem. The argument is an induction on the dimension \(n\), and each step leans on the two facts above.

Proof. The base case \(n = 1\) is immediate, since a \(1\times 1\) matrix is already diagonal. For the inductive step, Lemma 1 hands us a genuine real eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) with a unit eigenvector \(q_1\). Consider its orthogonal complement \(q_1^{\perp}\), the hyperplane of everything perpendicular to \(q_1\). Identity Equation 1 shows this hyperplane is \(A\)-invariant: if \(v \perp q_1\) then \(Av \perp q_1\) as well, so \(A\) never pushes you off the hyperplane. Restricted there, \(A\) is again symmetric but acts on a space of dimension \(n-1\), so the inductive hypothesis supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis of that smaller space. Adjoining \(q_1\) completes it to an orthonormal eigenbasis of all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Lining those vectors up as the columns of \(Q\) gives exactly Equation 2. \(\qquad\blacksquare\)

For a complete and careful treatment, including the version for self-adjoint operators on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, see [1]. For the numerical side of the story, [2] is the classic reference.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
A numerical check
A proof tells you a decomposition must exist; it is a different kind of satisfying to watch it appear. Let us build a random symmetric matrix, ask the computer for its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and confirm that Equation 2 holds right down to floating-point roundoff.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 6
M = rng.standard_normal((n, n))
A = (M + M.T) / 2                      # force symmetry

eigvals, Q = np.linalg.eigh(A)         # eigh is built for symmetric matrices
Lambda = np.diag(eigvals)

reconstruction_error = np.linalg.norm(A - Q @ Lambda @ Q.T)
orthogonality_error  = np.linalg.norm(Q.T @ Q - np.eye(n))

print(f"eigenvalues (all real): {np.round(eigvals, 4)}")
print(f"|A - Q L Q^T| = {reconstruction_error:.2e}")
print(f"|Q^T Q - I|   = {orthogonality_error:.2e}")

eigenvalues (all real): [-2.0037 -0.988   0.2761  0.4913  1.5001  1.8151]
|A - Q L Q^T| = 1.62e-15
|Q^T Q - I|   = 1.39e-15


Both residuals sit around \(10^{-15}\), which is as close to zero as double-precision arithmetic ever gets. The eigenvalues come back real, the eigenvectors come back orthonormal, and the stretch-and-rotate story holds up.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
What to remember
If you keep only three things from this note, keep these. Symmetry is really self-adjointness, the identity Equation 1, and that one fact is the engine of the entire proof. From it follow real eigenvalues (Lemma 1) and perpendicular eigenvectors (Lemma 2), which together build the orthonormal frame the theorem promises. And in practice, when you actually compute, reach for a symmetry-aware routine like eigh rather than the general eig; it is faster and it guarantees the real, orthogonal answer the mathematics says you deserve.

title: Quaternions: Seeing Four Dimensions with Three-Dimensional Eyes
text:
“Here as he walked by on the 16th of October 1843, Sir William Rowan Hamilton, in a flash of genius, discovered the fundamental formula for quaternion multiplication \(i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1\) & cut it on a stone of this bridge.”
— plaque on Broom Bridge, Dublin
Quaternions have a public relations problem that is almost two centuries old. They are four-dimensional numbers, which already sounds like a provocation; their multiplication refuses to commute, which feels like a betrayal; and the standard introduction — here is a table, \(ij = k\), \(ji = -k\), memorize it — manages to make one of the most geometric objects in mathematics feel like an arbitrary list of rules. If you have met quaternions before and bounced off, the problem was almost certainly not you.
This post makes two promises. The first is about logic: I want to show you that almost nothing about the quaternions is arbitrary — not the strange dimension count, not the multiplication rules, not even the failure of commutativity. Each is forced, step by inevitable step, the moment you ask one innocent question about multiplying points in space. The second is about sight: by the end, I want you to be able to read a product like \(i \cdot j = k\) and watch a specific, rigid motion of a four-dimensional sphere, using nothing but your three-dimensional imagination.

title: Quaternions: Seeing Four Dimensions with Three-Dimensional Eyes
section: A flash of genius on a Dublin bridge
text:
A flash of genius on a Dublin bridge
By the 1830s, mathematicians had made peace with complex numbers, and more than peace — they had fallen in love. A number \(a + bi\) is a point in the plane, and multiplication by it rotates and stretches that plane. Algebra and plane geometry turned out to be two languages for one thing. The Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton was gripped by the obvious next question: we live in three dimensions, so where is the number system for space?
He searched for over a decade. The story goes that his sons would ask at breakfast, “Papa, can you multiply triplets?” and he would shake his head: “No, I can only add and subtract them.” Then, on October 16th, 1843, walking along the Royal Canal, he saw it in a flash: the answer was not to add one imaginary axis to the complex numbers but two — three imaginary units \(i\), \(j\), \(k\) for space, bound to a real axis standing perpendicular to all of them. He scratched the governing law into the stone of Broom Bridge,
\[
i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1,
\tag{1}\]
and announced the discovery to the world within weeks [1]. He called the new numbers quaternions, and what followed is one of the great turf wars in the history of mathematics. Hamilton — and after him an actual official society — pushed quaternions as the language of three-dimensional science. The opposition produced some genuinely magnificent trash talk: Lord Kelvin wrote that quaternions, “though beautifully ingenious, have been an unmixed evil to those who have touched them in any way.” There is even a theory, taken half-seriously by historians, that the Mad Hatter’s endless rotation around the tea table — written, remember, by an Oxford mathematician — is a satire of their order-sensitive multiplication.
The vector calculus of Gibbs and Heaviside won the textbooks, and we will see in a moment that it won them by strip-mining Hamilton’s formula. But the twentieth century staged two rescues: computer graphics and robotics rediscovered that quaternions encode 3D rotations more compactly and stably than anything else — your phone and every spacecraft attitude controller multiply them constantly — and quantum mechanics found that the algebra of a spinning electron is Hamilton’s algebra in a lab coat. Numbers this inevitable do not stay buried.
So let’s do what Hamilton could not do on the bridge, with no flash of genius required: walk the logic slowly enough that four dimensions become the obvious answer.

title: Quaternions: Seeing Four Dimensions with Three-Dimensional Eyes
text:
The innocent question
What should “multiplying points” even mean? Let’s write down our demands honestly, because everything follows from them. We have points in some \(n\)-dimensional space, we can already add them and scale them, and we want a multiplication such that, first, it distributes over addition the way any self-respecting product does; second, we can divide — every nonzero point has a reciprocal; and third, it respects geometry. That last demand has a precise, modest form. Every point \(q\) has a size \(|q|\), its distance from the origin, and we ask that
\[
|q_1 q_2| \;=\; |q_1|\,|q_2|.
\tag{2}\]
Lengths multiply. That is all. It looks like a throwaway technicality, and it is in fact the steel beam holding up everything in this post.
Watch what Equation 2 already does in two dimensions. Write the squared length of \((a,b)\) as \(a^2 + b^2\). If a length-respecting multiplication exists, then the product of two sums of two squares must again be a sum of two squares — and it is, by an identity that was known to Diophantus seventeen centuries before complex numbers existed:
\[
(a^2 + b^2)(c^2 + d^2) \;=\; (ac - bd)^2 + (ad + bc)^2.
\tag{3}\]
Now look closely at the right-hand side. The expressions \(ac - bd\) and \(ad + bc\) are precisely the real and imaginary parts of the product \((a + bi)(c + di)\). The multiplication rule of complex numbers is not a convention someone chose; it is the unique way to factor the two-square identity. The algebra was hiding inside an arithmetic fact all along. Take a moment with that — it is the cleanest example I know of a number system being discovered rather than invented.

title: Quaternions: Seeing Four Dimensions with Three-Dimensional Eyes
text:
Why three dimensions refuse
So Hamilton’s program needs a three-square identity: the product of two sums of three squares should be a sum of three squares. And here the universe says no, and it says it with a concrete counterexample rather than abstract hand-wringing. Both \(3 = 1^2 + 1^2 + 1^2\) and \(5 = 0^2 + 1^2 + 2^2\) are sums of three squares. Their product is \(15\) — and \(15\) simply is not. Try it: \(9 + 4 + 1\) overshoots at \(14\), every other combination misses too. (Number theorists know the full story: integers of the form \(8b + 7\) refuse to be three squares, and \(15\) is the smallest product to weaponize this.)
Sit with what just happened. A fact about the integer \(15\) reaches up and forbids an entire algebra. No bilinear, length-respecting multiplication of 3D points can exist, no matter how clever you are, because if it did, Equation 2 would manufacture a three-square identity and \(15\) stands in the way. Hamilton’s decade of frustration was not a failure of imagination — he was pushing against a theorem.
But Euler, a century before Hamilton, had found that four squares work [2]:
\[
(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)(e^2+f^2+g^2+h^2) = (ae-bf-cg-dh)^2 + (af+be+ch-dg)^2 + (ag-bh+ce+df)^2 + (ah+bg-cf+de)^2.
\tag{4}\]
At first glance this looks like a wall of symbols, but you have already seen its little sibling Equation 3 and you know how to read it: those four expressions on the right are a multiplication rule trying to be born. Factor the four-square identity the way the two-square identity factors, and the structure constants of Equation 1 fall out — not chosen, forced. The quaternions had been waiting inside Euler’s identity since 1748, ninety-five years before Hamilton heard them knocking. And the pattern stops where it stops for a reason: Hurwitz proved in 1898 that such identities exist only for \(n = 1, 2, 4, 8\) — reals, complexes, quaternions, and (by the way, with division but at the price of associativity) the eight-dimensional octonions, after which the door closes forever [2]. The dimension four was never strange. It was one of the only four options the integers ever put on the table.

title: Quaternions: Seeing Four Dimensions with Three-Dimensional Eyes
section: The product that contains a geometry course
text:
The product that contains a geometry course
Now let’s actually hold the multiplication in our hands, because it has more inside it than its definition suggests. Split a quaternion into Hamilton’s two parts: a real number plus a 3D point, \(q = a + \mathbf{v}\). Hamilton needed a name for that pure spatial part, the piece spanned by \(i, j, k\), and the word he coined was vector — the everyday word is a fossil of this exact construction. Multiply two quaternions \((a + \mathbf{v})(b + \mathbf{w})\) by brute distribution using Equation 1, collect terms, and the result organizes itself into something startling:
\[
(a + \mathbf{v})(b + \mathbf{w}) \;=\; \underbrace{ab - \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w}}_{\text{real part}} \;+\; \underbrace{a\,\mathbf{w} + b\,\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w}}_{\text{vector part}}.
\tag{5}\]
Look at what surfaced: the dot product and the cross product, both of them, with their signs and their geometry, born as the real and vector shrapnel of a single quaternion product. This is not an analogy — it is ancestry. Gibbs and Heaviside built vector analysis by taking Equation 5 apart and keeping the pieces; the dot and cross products you learned as separate gadgets are the two halves of one multiplication that predates them both. Doesn’t that just feel beautiful? Every identity that mixes dot and cross products is secretly a statement about associativity in Hamilton’s algebra.
And the famous rules are now corollaries you can see. For pure vectors the real parts vanish, so \(\mathbf{v}\mathbf{w} = -\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w}\). Take \(\mathbf{v} = i\), \(\mathbf{w} = j\): perpendicular, so the dot part is zero, and \(i \times j = k\). Hence \(ij = k\). Swap the order and the cross product flips sign: \(ji = -k\). The notorious non-commutativity of quaternions is nothing but the antisymmetry of the cross product — which is itself the honest geometric fact that orientation matters in space. A number system that truly speaks for 3D geometry had no choice but to give up commutativity; a commutative one would have been lying about space. Even \(\mathbf{v}^2 = -|\mathbf{v}|^2\), the rule that every unit vector is a square root of \(-1\), falls out of Equation 5 in one line.
That last sentence deserves its own paragraph, because it quietly hands us the entire shape of what comes next. Every unit vector \(\mathbf{u}\) — not just \(i\) — satisfies \(\mathbf{u}^2 = -1\). So inside the quaternions, the plane spanned by \(1\) and \(\mathbf{u}\) is a perfect copy of the complex numbers, and every unit quaternion can be written as
\[
q \;=\; \cos\theta + \mathbf{u}\sin\theta,
\tag{6}\]
an “\(e^{i\theta}\)” with a choice of which \(i\). The unit quaternions are a book whose pages are complex unit circles, all bound together along the spine \(\{1, -1\}\), one page for every direction \(\mathbf{u}\) in space.

title: Quaternions: Seeing Four Dimensions with Three-Dimensional Eyes
section: The shape of the unit quaternions
text:
The shape of the unit quaternions
Where do those unit quaternions live? In four coordinates \((a,b,c,d)\) with \(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2 = 1\): the unit hypersphere \(S^3\), a three-dimensional surface curving through four-dimensional space. And Equation 2 gives this sphere a property that ordinary spheres can only envy: the product of two unit quaternions is again a unit quaternion. The hypersphere is closed under multiplication — it is a group, a space whose every point is also a motion of that space. Among all spheres of all dimensions, essentially only the circle \(S^1\) and this hypersphere \(S^3\) carry such a structure. The circle’s multiplication runs the theory of angles and Fourier series; its big sibling’s multiplication runs the theory of spatial rotation. We have walked into very select company.
So the object of study is fixed: a 4D sphere we cannot see, on which multiplication acts by — what, exactly? By Equation 2, multiplying by a unit quaternion preserves all lengths: it is a rigid rotation of four-dimensional space. The two promises of this post have become one task. See the hypersphere; watch it turn.

title: Quaternions: Seeing Four Dimensions with Three-Dimensional Eyes
text:
Borrowing eyes
Here is the move, and it is a move worth owning for life: when a space has one dimension too many for your eyes, ask how you would show your world to a creature with one dimension too few — then accept the same charity from above. Mathematicians have a precise instrument for this, stereographic projection, and we will rehearse it twice before using it in earnest.
Rehearsal one: show a circle to a creature who knows only a line. The unit complex numbers form a circle; rotation is its native motion; and a rotation has just one degree of freedom, so a line ought to suffice to display it. Project from the point \(-1\): for each other point of the circle, draw the straight line from \(-1\) through it and mark where it crosses the tangent line at the opposite pole. The point \(1\) lands at the center; \(i\) and \(-i\) stay put; arcs near \(-1\) fly off toward the two infinite ends, and \(-1\) itself becomes the point at infinity. Now multiply the circle by \(i\) — a crisp quarter turn — and watch its shadow: the center point slides to \(i\), the point at \(i\) flees off the end of the line, infinity wraps around and re-enters at \(-i\), and four repetitions bring every point home: \(i^4 = 1\), visible. The motion looks stretchy and strange, but that is the lens, not the motion. Holding those two truths at once — the shadow distorts, the object is rigid — is the entire skill.
Rehearsal two: show a rotating sphere to a creature who knows only a plane, and — this is the version we need — build the sphere out of number axes: real axis vertical, two imaginary axes \(i, j\) spanning the floor. Project the unit sphere from its south pole \(-1\) onto the floor. The north pole \(1\) lands at the origin. The equator through \(\pm i, \pm j\) is already in the floor and does not move: one honest, undistorted circle amid the shadows. The northern hemisphere (positive real part) lands inside it, the southern outside, and \(-1\) is again the point at infinity. One dictionary entry pays for the whole rehearsal: every straight line the flat creature sees is the shadow of a circle through \(-1\). A line is a circle through infinity. Once that clicks, a rotation that appears to deform a circle into a line stops being alarming — upstairs it is just a circle turning rigidly through the south pole. Spin the sphere a quarter turn about the \(j\)-axis (\(1 \to i \to -1 \to -i\)) and the flat creature sees, embedded along one line of their floor, exactly the lurching motion of rehearsal one, while the honest circle swings up into a vertical line. Nothing stretched. It never does.
Now the real thing, with practiced eyes. Project the hypersphere of unit quaternions from \(-1\) into our 3D space. The number \(1\) lands at the center of the room. The “equator” — all unit quaternions with zero real part, which is exactly the sphere of unit vectors through \(i, j, k\) — lies in our space already and projects to itself: an honest unit sphere around the origin, the one fully trustworthy object in view. Unit quaternions with positive real part fill the inside of that sphere; negative real parts land outside; \(-1\) is the point at infinity, in every direction at once. And the dictionary carries up a dimension: every plane through the origin is secretly a great sphere through \(-1\); every line through the origin is secretly a great circle through \(-1\). The line you see through \(1\), \(i\), \(-i\) is the unit circle of the complex numbers — one page of the book from Equation 6, lying open in the room. Pause here until the sentence “everything I see is at distance exactly \(1\) from a number zero that is nowhere in the picture” stops hurting. It does stop.

title: Quaternions: Seeing Four Dimensions with Three-Dimensional Eyes
text:
Watching the multiplication
What does left-multiplication by a unit quaternion do to this picture? Here is the answer, and every clause of it is now checkable with your own eyes:

Multiplying on the left by \(q = \cos\theta + \mathbf{u}\sin\theta\) rotates the complex circle of \(\mathbf{u}\) — the circle through \(1\), \(\mathbf{u}\), \(-1\), seen by us as a line through the origin — by the angle \(\theta\), carrying \(1\) to \(q\). Simultaneously, it rotates the great circle perpendicular to it, lying on the honest sphere, by the same angle \(\theta\).

Two completely perpendicular circles — same center, same radius, no common point, a configuration that sounds impossible until you grant them four dimensions to dodge each other in — turning in lockstep. Rotations with this equal-angle property are called isoclinic, and they exist only in four dimensions and above. In 3D every rotation has an axis, a line of points left alone; this motion fixes nothing whatsoever. (I first learned to actually see this picture, with the projected hypersphere and the hand gestures below, from Grant Sanderson’s video on the subject [3] — the debt for the visual language of this section is his.)
Make it concrete with \(q = i\), so \(\mathbf{u} = i\) and \(\theta = 90^\circ\). The circle through \(1\) and \(i\) appears as a line through the origin, and along it runs the lurch you have now rehearsed twice: \(1 \to i\), \(i \to -1\) (off to infinity), \(-1 \to -i\) (back in from beyond), \(-i \to 1\). Meanwhile the perpendicular great circle through \(j\) and \(k\), sitting on the honest sphere, turns \(90^\circ\) in the direction given by a right-hand rule: point your right thumb from \(1\) toward \(i\) along the visible line, and your fingers curl the way the \(jk\)-circle rolls. Read the products straight off the motion:
\[
i \cdot 1 = i, \qquad i \cdot i = -1, \qquad i \cdot j = k, \qquad i \cdot k = -j.
\]
My honest hope is that this is no longer a table but a film: the line flowing, the circle rolling with your curled fingers, four frames returning everything home because \(i^4 = 1\). And since multiplication distributes, knowing the motion on the basis \(1, i, j, k\) pins it down on every quaternion — see the action on four points, know it on the whole 4D space. For a general \(q\) the recipe never changes: draw the circle through \(1\), \(q\), \(-1\); turn it until \(1\) reaches \(q\); turn the perpendicular circle on the honest sphere by the same angle, right-handedly. One point of the hypersphere chosen, one rigid motion determined. The two computations \(ij = k\) and \(ji = -k\) are now two genuinely different films — thumb toward \(i\) curling \(j\) up to \(k\), versus thumb toward \(j\) curling \(i\) down to \(-k\) — and non-commutativity is something your hands knew before your algebra did. It is the same lesson the cross product whispered earlier, now playing on the big screen.

title: Quaternions: Seeing Four Dimensions with Three-Dimensional Eyes
text:
Two hands, all of rotation
One refinement opens the door to everything quaternions are used for. You can also multiply by \(q\) on the right, and the motion is the mirror twin: the same circle through \(1, q, -1\) turns the same way, but the perpendicular circle now obeys a left-hand rule. Left multiplications and right multiplications are two distinct families of isoclinic rotations — and here is the theorem that I find quietly astonishing: composing them, \(x \mapsto p\,x\,q\), produces every rotation of four-dimensional space, and essentially uniquely [2]. The entire rotation group of 4D, an object you might expect to be hopelessly opaque, factors into a left hand and a right hand, each one a copy of our hypersphere.
And now you can feel the next chapter coming. A single multiplication tilts the honest sphere of vectors off through the fourth dimension — beautiful, but not yet a rotation of space. The fix is to let the two hands collaborate against each other: the sandwich \(\mathbf{v} \mapsto q\,\mathbf{v}\,q^{-1}\), one left action and one right action whose off-sphere tilts cancel exactly, leaving the honest sphere turning rigidly in place. That sandwich is how your phone, your game engine, and your favorite spacecraft actually compute rotations, and it hides one more elegant secret — \(q\) and \(-q\) perform the same rotation, a two-to-one disguise called the double cover, which is precisely the mathematics of electron spin. Unpacking it properly deserves its own post, and it will get one.
Until then, sit with what the innocent question bought us: lengths multiply, so \(15\) forbids three dimensions, so Euler’s identity forces four; the product, once forced, births the dot and cross products and pays for non-commutativity with honest geometry; the unit quaternions close into one of the only spheres in mathematics that is also a group; and its multiplication, seen through a projection we borrowed by climbing down two dimensions and back up, is a pair of perpendicular circles turning as one. If you want to hold the hypersphere in your own hands, Sanderson and Eater built an explorable version of these pictures that you can drag around yourself [4] — go play. The “unmixed evil” was geometry all along, waiting a century and a half for someone to draw it.

title: Prime Spirals
text:
“A mathematician, like a painter or a poet, is a maker of patterns. If his patterns are more permanent than theirs, it is because they are made with ideas.”
— G. H. Hardy, A Mathematician’s Apology (1940)
Some of the best mathematics I know starts with a completely pointless act. Here is one: take the prime numbers \(2, 3, 5, 7, 11, \dots\) and plot each prime \(p\) in polar coordinates at the point \((r, \theta) = (p, p)\) — its distance from the origin is \(p\), and its angle, measured in radians, is also \(p\). There is no reason to do this. Radians and radii have nothing to do with primality; we are just feeding the same number into two slots because the slots are there.
And yet, zoom out, and the dots arrange themselves into a galaxy: dozens of spiral arms swirling out from the center, with whole sectors gone dark, as if some arms had been deleted. Zoom out further and the spirals straighten into crisp rays shooting outward — mostly bundled in groups of four, like the teeth of a comb, with the occasional tooth snapped off.
The first time you see this (I met it through Grant Sanderson’s video on the phenomenon [1]), it is hard not to suspect you’ve stumbled onto some secret structure of the primes. The truth is better than that. The pattern is a kind of optical illusion — but decoding the illusion, piece by piece, walks you straight through some of the most beautiful ideas in number theory, ending at a genuine landmark: Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions. Let’s take the walk.

title: Prime Spirals
text:
The phenomenon
First, look at the thing itself. Here are the primes plotted at \((p, p)\), at three zoom levels.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def primes_upto(n):
    sieve = np.ones(n + 1, dtype=bool); sieve[:2] = False
    for k in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[k]:
            sieve[k*k::k] = False
    return np.flatnonzero(sieve)

p = primes_upto(300_000)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.5, 3.5),
                         subplot_kw={"projection": "polar"})
for ax, lim, s in zip(axes, [3_000, 30_000, 300_000], [3, 0.6, 0.15]):
    q = p[p < lim]
    ax.scatter(q % (2*np.pi), q, s=s, color="#1f4e79", lw=0)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_title(f"primes up to {lim:,}", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 1: Primes \(p\) plotted at polar coordinates \((r, \theta) = (p, p)\). Left: spiral arms, with gaps where arms seem to be missing. Middle: the transition. Right: the spirals straighten into rays, grouped like comb teeth.





Take a moment with the left panel. Count the arms, notice the dark wedges where arms ought to be. Then look at the right panel: straight rays, in tidy clusters of four, and — squint — every so often a ray missing, a broken tooth in the comb.
Two mysteries, then. Why spirals and rays at all? And who is deleting the missing ones?

title: Prime Spirals
section: Mystery one: the spirals are not about primes
text:
Mystery one: the spirals are not about primes
Here is the move that cracks the whole thing open, and it’s the oldest trick in the debugging handbook: change one thing at a time. What happens if we drop the primality requirement and plot every whole number at \((n, n)\)?

lim = 3_000
n = np.arange(1, lim)
q = p[p < lim]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4),
                         subplot_kw={"projection": "polar"})
for ax, pts, title in [(axes[0], n, "all integers"),
                       (axes[1], q, "primes only")]:
    ax.scatter(pts % (2*np.pi), pts, s=2, color="#1f4e79", lw=0)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 2: The same window, with all integers (left) and primes only (right). The spirals belong to the integers; the primes merely inherit them — minus some arms.





The spirals are still there — denser, cleaner, with every arm intact. So the swirling structure has nothing to do with primes whatsoever. It is a geometric by-product of how all whole numbers land when you spin them around the origin. The primes are just along for the ride, occupying a subset of the arms. That immediately splits our investigation in two: first understand why integers make spirals, then understand which arms the primes are allowed to ride.
So: why do the integers make spirals? Walk the sequence step by step. Going from \(n\) to \(n+1\) moves you one unit further out and one radian further around. A radian is just a hair less than a sixth of a full turn, because a full turn is \(2\pi \approx 6.283\) radians. So watch what happens after six steps: you have rotated by \(6\) radians — almost, but not quite, a full circle, falling short by about \(0.283\) radians.
Hold that picture. The number \(n + 6\) lands at almost the same angle as \(n\), just one notch further out and rotated back a sliver. And \(n + 12\) repeats the trick, and \(n + 18\), and so on. Each chain of numbers spaced \(6\) apart forms a gently curving arm. How many such chains are there? Exactly six — one for each possible remainder upon dividing by \(6\). The six spiral arms you see near the origin are nothing more than the residue classes mod 6, rendered geometrically. The arms curve because \(6\) is a good-but-not-great approximation of \(2\pi\); the leftover \(0.283\) radians per cycle is the twist.
This kind of pattern shows up all the time in mathematics: a near-miss between two periods creates a slow drift. (It’s the same reason the moon shows us slightly different faces over a month, and the same beat phenomenon you hear when two guitar strings are almost in tune.)
Now, can we do better than “six steps is almost a turn”? Ask the question properly: we want whole numbers \(a\) and \(b\) with \(a\) radians very close to \(b\) full turns — that is, \(\frac{a}{b} \approx 2\pi\). This is the classical problem of rational approximation, and \(\pi\) has two famous star approximations. You might have already guessed the first: \(\pi \approx \frac{22}{7}\). Doubling it, \(\frac{44}{7} \approx 2\pi\), which says that 44 steps make almost exactly 7 full turns, overshooting by a mere \(0.0177\) radians. So at a medium zoom, the integers organize themselves into \(44\) chains — the residue classes mod \(44\) — and because the per-cycle twist is so tiny, these \(44\) arms curve far more gently than the six did. That is the galaxy in the left panel.
And the second star: the stunning approximation \(\pi \approx \frac{355}{113}\), known in China as Zu Chongzhi’s milü, accurate to six decimal places. Doubling: \(\frac{710}{113} \approx 2\pi\), i.e. 710 steps make almost exactly 113 full turns, with an error around \(6 \times 10^{-5}\) radians. At this scale the residual twist is invisible — a curvature so slight your screen cannot render it — and the \(710\) residue classes mod \(710\) appear as 710 dead-straight rays. That is the right panel.
Pause and chew on this, because it’s the heart of mystery one: the spirals-then-rays progression is just the continued fraction expansion of \(2\pi\) made visible. Each zoom level snaps to the best rational approximation available at that scale — \(\frac{6}{1}\), then \(\frac{44}{7}\), then \(\frac{710}{113}\) — and the quality of the approximation controls how straight the arms look. A pointless doodle, and it hands you rational approximation theory unprompted.

title: Prime Spirals
text:
Mystery two: the missing arms
Back to the primes, and to the deleted arms. Remember what an arm is: all the numbers with a fixed remainder mod \(6\) (or \(44\), or \(710\)). So asking “which arms survive in the prime picture?” is asking: which remainders can a prime have?
Start small, with mod \(6\). A number with remainder \(0\), \(2\), or \(4\) is even; remainder \(3\) means divisible by \(3\). None of those arms can contain a prime — except the lone primes \(2\) and \(3\) themselves, a single dot each, invisible at any zoom. Primes can only live on the arms with remainder \(1\) or \(5\), the remainders that share no factor with \(6\). Six arms, four deleted, two survive. If you plot primes up to a few hundred you see exactly two spiral arms.
The same sieve explains the galaxy’s dark sectors. We have \(44 = 4 \times 11\). Any arm whose remainder is even is wiped out; so is any arm whose remainder is a multiple of \(11\). Count the survivors: of the \(44\) residue classes, only the \(20\) that are coprime to 44 can host primes. Twenty arms out of forty-four — nearly half the galaxy goes dark, in whole wedges at a time. Go back and count the arms in the first figure’s left panel: twenty.
And now the comb. We have \(710 = 2 \times 5 \times 71\), and each prime factor leaves its own distinctive fingerprint on the picture:

The factor 2 deletes every even ray — half the comb gone, leaving \(355\) rays that alternate with gaps. This is why the surviving rays come in evenly spaced pairs of neighbors-but-one.
The factor 5 deletes every fifth ray among the survivors. Knock out one ray in five, and the remaining rays cluster into groups of four — there is the comb-teeth pattern, explained.
The factor 71 deletes a sparse, irregular-looking sprinkle: only \(1\) ray in \(71\). That is the occasional broken tooth — rare enough to look like a glitch, lawful enough to be a theorem.

How many rays survive in total? The count of numbers from \(1\) to \(710\) sharing no factor with \(710\). This quantity is important enough to carry a name and a symbol: Euler’s totient function \(\phi(n)\). For a product of distinct primes it peels off one factor at a time,
\[
\phi(710) = 710 \cdot \Big(1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\Big)\Big(1 - \tfrac{1}{5}\Big)\Big(1 - \tfrac{1}{71}\Big) = 280,
\]
so of the \(710\) rays, exactly \(280\) can carry primes. Both mysteries are now solved: the arms come from rational approximations of \(2\pi\), and the missing ones are the residue classes that flunk a coprimality test. By the way — notice that we have rediscovered, in order, modular arithmetic, rational approximation, and the totient function, without once opening a textbook. The doodle has been a better syllabus than most syllabi.

title: Prime Spirals
text:
The real question, hiding underneath
But wait — solving the two mysteries has quietly exposed a third, and it is much deeper. Look again at the right panel of the first figure. The \(280\) surviving rays don’t just contain primes; they look equally bright. No surviving ray seems privileged. Is that real? Do the primes truly spread themselves evenly across all the residue classes they are allowed to occupy?
At first glance there is no reason they should. Being coprime to \(710\) makes a ray eligible, but eligibility is not equality — the primes could have favorites. Let’s interrogate the simplest possible case: \(n = 10\). A prime bigger than \(5\) must end in \(1\), \(3\), \(7\), or \(9\) (the four digits coprime to \(10\)). Are the four endings equally popular?

P = primes_upto(2_000_000)
P = P[P > 5]
x = np.logspace(2, np.log10(2_000_000), 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for d in (1, 3, 7, 9):
    counts = np.searchsorted(P[P % 10 == d], x)
    total  = np.searchsorted(P, x)
    ax.plot(x, counts / total, lw=1.5, label=f"last digit {d}")
ax.axhline(0.25, color="gray", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_ylim(0.15, 0.35)
ax.set_xlabel("upper bound $x$")
ax.set_ylabel("share of primes $\\leq x$")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncols=2)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 3: Among all primes up to \(x\), the share ending in each of the four allowed digits. The four curves squeeze toward exactly 25% each.





The early data is noisy, the way small numbers always are. But as \(x\) grows, the four shares are squeezed inexorably toward \(25\%\) each. The primes, for all their famous lawlessness, are scrupulously fair about their last digits.
This is no accident of base ten, and proving it is one of the great achievements of nineteenth-century mathematics. In 1837, Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet proved what is now called Dirichlet’s theorem on arithmetic progressions [2]: for any modulus \(n\) and any remainder \(a\) coprime to \(n\), there are infinitely many primes congruent to \(a\) mod \(n\) — and more than that, the primes distribute themselves with equal density among all \(\phi(n)\) allowed classes.1 In the language of our picture: every one of the \(280\) surviving rays carries, in the limit, exactly \(\frac{1}{280}\) of all primes. The uniform glow is a theorem.
What I find most striking is how Dirichlet proved it. The statement is as discrete as mathematics gets — counting whole numbers with no divisors, sorted by remainders. Yet the proof reaches across the aisle and grabs the machinery of continuous mathematics: infinite series, complex-valued functions (now called Dirichlet \(L\)-functions), and arguments where the key fact is that a certain function does not vanish at a certain point [3]. This crossing of the discrete–continuous border was the founding act of analytic number theory, and the border has been busy ever since: the same family of ideas — primes in residue classes, and how evenly they fill them — sits at the center of the modern assault on the twin prime conjecture, where results about bounded gaps between primes lean precisely on strong forms of equidistribution in arithmetic progressions. The question our doodle raised by accident is, quite literally, frontier mathematics.

title: Prime Spirals
text:
What the doodle knew
Let’s step back and admire what just happened. We plotted primes in polar coordinates for no reason at all. The pattern that emerged was, in a strict sense, fake — the spirals belonged to all integers, the gaps to garden-variety divisibility. Not one pixel of the picture was special to the primes… except the one feature we almost took for granted: the evenness of the glow along the surviving rays, which turned out to be Dirichlet’s theorem in disguise.
And that, I think, is the real lesson, the reason to cherish pointless plots. Worked through honestly, one idle visualization forced us to rediscover residue classes, the continued-fraction approximations \(\frac{22}{7}\) and \(\frac{355}{113}\), Euler’s totient function, and the threshold of analytic number theory. Every one of those ideas also sits, definition-first and motivation-last, in a textbook chapter — where it is so easy to memorize and forget. Met this way, as answers to questions you actually asked while staring at a picture you actually cared about, they arrive as old friends. You don’t have to remember them, because now they are part of how you see.
So: go plot something for no reason. The math underneath is patient, and it knows how to introduce itself.

title: Prime Spirals
text:
What to remember
The prime spiral is two theorems wearing a costume. The spiral arms are rational approximation — \(6\), then \(\frac{44}{7}\), then \(\frac{710}{113}\) chasing \(2\pi\) through its continued fraction. The missing arms are coprimality, counted by \(\phi(n)\). And the one honest mystery in the picture — that the surviving arms shine equally — is Dirichlet’s theorem: primes fill every allowed residue class with the same density, \(\frac{1}{\phi(n)}\).
